bib.title: The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context

read.skipped: Supplementary Material (hyperparameter tuning, filter-model details) is not in the PDF; it is hosted at clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/

question: Can a word-prediction benchmark be built whose targets humans guess from a broad passage but not from the last sentence alone, and how do language models of 2016 fare on it?
hypothesis: Models that only use local context cannot solve items that need broad discourse context; LAMBADA should expose this.
contributions: LAMBADA, 10,022 narrative passages whose last word is human-guessable only with the full passage
Analysis of the linguistic phenomena in the data
Evaluation of N-gram, RNN, LSTM, Memory Network and baselines, none above 1% accuracy

method.summary: Passages from the Book Corpus are filtered with four language models, then with a three-step CrowdFlower protocol (two subjects must guess the final word from the whole passage; none of up to ten may guess it from the last sentence alone). Several language models trained on 2,662 novels are scored on accuracy, perplexity and median rank of the target word.
method.task: final-word prediction in narrative passages (language modelling with broad context)

datasets.name: Book Corpus (filtered)
datasets.split: novels split into equal halves: training 2,662 novels (>200M words, 203 million words) and dev+test
datasets.source: Zhu et al., 2015 Book Corpus (unpublished novels)
datasets.preprocessing: duplicate removal; offensive material filtered with a stop word list

datasets.name: LAMBADA
datasets.size: 10,022 passages; average 4.6 context sentences plus 1 target sentence, 75.4 tokens (dev) / 75 tokens (test)
datasets.split: 4,869 dev (1,331 novels) and 5,153 test (1,332 disjoint novels)
datasets.source: dev+test half of the Book Corpus novels
datasets.preprocessing: context = minimum whole sentences before target sentence totalling at least 50 tokens; target = last word of the target sentence; LM filter drops any passage where any of 4 LMs gives the target probability >= 0.00175

datasets.name: Control set
datasets.size: 5K passages of the same shape and size, unfiltered
datasets.split: sampled from the same test novels

models.name: LSTM
models.architecture: LSTM LM, similar to Deep LSTM Reader

models.name: Memory Network
models.architecture: similar to Hill et al. 2016 CBT best system

models.name: Sup-CBOW
models.architecture: simple neural net over summed pre-trained CBOW vectors of passage words

other.train_passages: about 9M passages of LAMBADA shape from the training novels

models.name: Unsup-CBOW
models.architecture: cosine similarity between passage vector and target word vector

models.name: Filter LMs
models.architecture: pre-trained RNN (Mikolov 2011) plus 4-gram, RNN, feed-forward trained on Book Corpus

other.note: used only to filter candidates; differ from evaluated models

training.objective: predict each upcoming word given previous context on the training novels (Sup-CBOW: predict final word of passage)

inference.decoding: rank vocabulary by model probability; correct if the target is the top word

limits: Authors call the model evaluation 'very preliminary' and a 'proof-of-concept'; more tuning or attention might do better.
Standard LMs fail 'by design' because the dataset was filtered to passages where four simple LMs gave the target probability below 0.00175.
Strict exact-match human criterion excludes passages with synonymous or alternative plausible answers.
Hyperparameters, model sizes and optimiser are in the Supplementary Material, not the paper; the PDF does not say whether Table 1 uses dev or test.
Targets skew to proper nouns (48%) and to words present in context (>80%), so co-reference is over-represented; script/event reasoning is underrepresented.
Dated: the 1% ceiling applies to 2016 RNN/n-gram/memory models; later large LMs score far higher (not in this paper).
